title: The people of the bench
hookLine: poor companions live on a shaded platform in the mosque, learning (Bukhari)

cards: Too many hadith. Some people grumbled that Abu Hurayra reported too many sayings of the Prophet, a complaint old enough to be answered inside Sahih al-Bukhari, by Abu Hurayra himself.
His answer is about where he spent his days. His brothers among the emigrants, he says, were busy trading in the markets. His brothers among the people of Medina were busy working their property.

And he stayed close to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, content with whatever filled his stomach, present when others were away, remembering what others forgot. Today: ahl al-suffah, the people of the bench.

teach.h: A SHADED PLATFORM IN THE MOSQUE.
teach.b: When the mosque of Medina was built, part of it had a covered, shaded platform. The Arabic word is suffah, and the people who lived there were called ahl al-suffah, the people of the bench. Who were they?
In another report in Bukhari, Abu Hurayra calls them the guests of Islam: people with no family to go to and no wealth to fall back on. The bench was their home, and the mosque was their school.
Bukhari also shows how they were fed.
When charity came to the Prophet, he sent it to them and took none of it himself. When a gift came, he shared in it with them.

In one long report, Abu Hurayra is so hungry he can barely stand, and the Prophet sends him to call the people of the bench to share a single bowl of milk. Abu Hurayra worries there'll be nothing left for him.

He serves them all, and in that story there's enough. The community put the people with the least in the middle of the mosque itself. Not at the edge of town, not out of sight, but beside the teaching.
And the poor weren't only receivers.
Because they stayed, they listened. Because they listened, they remembered. And Abu Hurayra, who stayed close while others were busy, became the man people asked why he had so many sayings to report.

how: Muslims remember ahl al-suffah as a model of learning and of caring for the poor, and some mosques and schools support students who live and study on site.

games.q: you're Abu Hurayra, faint with hunger. the Prophet hands you one bowl of milk and tells you to call all the people of the bench. what do you do?

games.why: he called them and served them all, worried there'd be none left, and in the story there was enough.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is learning right now and doesn't have much, a student you know, a young person in your family, someone retraining or studying their faith, and picture them on that bench.
What would help them stay close to what they're learning: a meal, a book, your time, a word of encouragement? If you pray, you can ask Allah to open their way.

wordCard.voice: Ahl al-suffah. The people of the bench: poor companions who lived on the shaded platform of the mosque in Medina, fed by charity, learning close to the Prophet. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: 'the people of the suffah', the shaded platform in the mosque of Medina.

carryVoice: Your line: the bench of the poor. Right in the middle of the mosque, not out of sight. That's today.
